Paper Content:
Towards Safe Path Tracking Using the Simplex Architecture
Georg Jäger1, Nils-Jonathan Friedrich1, Hauke Petersen2, Benjamin Noack2
Abstract— Robot navigation in complex environments necessitates controllers that are adaptive and safe. Traditional
controllers like Regulated Pure Pursuit, Dynamic Window
Approach, and Model-Predictive Path Integral, while reliable,
struggle to adapt to dynamic conditions. Reinforcement Learning offers adaptability but lacks formal safety guarantees. To
address this, we propose a path tracking controller leveraging the Simplex architecture. It combines a Reinforcement
Learning controller for adaptiveness and performance with a
high-assurance controller providing safety and stability. Our
contribution is twofold. We firstly discuss general stability
and safety considerations for designing controllers using the
Simplex architecture. Secondly, we present a Simplex-based
path tracking controller. Our simulation results, supported
by preliminary in-field tests, demonstrate the controller’s effectiveness in maintaining safety while achieving comparable
performance to state-of-the-art methods.
I. INTRODUCTION
Fig. 1: Autonomous mobile robot demonstrating parcel delivery on
a sidewalk of 2m width.
Autonomous mobile robots will revolutionize diverse applications, e.g., in logistics for parcel delivery cf. Fig. 1,
agriculture, healthcare, etc. [1]. A central capability for that
is effective navigation, which requires robots to follow a (pre-
)planned path. This task is typically addressed by path tracking algorithms. While traditional controllers like Dynamic
Window Approach Version B (DWB) [2], Model Predictive
Path Integral (MPPI) [3], and Regulated Pure Pursuit (RPP) [4],
[5] are performant in known, static environments [6], they
struggle in complex, dynamic environments due to limited
adaptability. For instance, RPP is simple and effective but

lacks adaptability due to its lookahead distance [4]. MPPI, a
model-based controller, can optimize to a given path while
considering the robot’s dynamics and constraints [3], but
requires precise system dynamics models and careful tuning,
hindering its adaptability to changing conditions. DWB, while
computationally efficient, can find suboptimal solutions due
to its limited planning horizon and reactive nature [2]. These
limitations highlight a key challenge: effectively parameterizing path tracking algorithms for complex, dynamic scenarios.
Reinforcement Learning (RL) offers an alternative and has
proven its performance and adaptability for path tracking [7],
[8], [9] as well as in other complex, dynamic application
scenarios [10]. However, the black-box nature of neural
networks commonly used in (deep) RL contradicts the need
for safety and stability guarantees. Hybrid architectures, such
as the Simplex architecture [11], aim to bridge this gap
by combining the performance of RL controllers with the
safety guarantees of traditional controllers. The RL controller
operates under normal conditions, while a high-assurance
fallback controller (e.g., DWB, MPPI, or RPP) ensures safety
when needed.
Despite their potential, hybrid architectures seem to be
underexplored in path tracking and autonomous navigation,
most notably in Robot Operating System Version 2 (ROS2).
To address this gap, we make two contributions. Firstly, we
discuss design considerations for ensuring safety and stability
in controllers using the Simplex architecture (cf. Section III).
Secondly, we present a Simplex-based path tracking controller (cf. Section IV), which employs an RL-based highperformance controller and a Pure Pursuit (PP)-based highassurance controller providing safety and stability guarantees. The controller is evaluated in simulations (cf. Section V), demonstrating its effectiveness in maintaining safety
while achieving comparable performance to state-of-the-art
methods, as well as in a real-world deployment. In the next
section, however, we start by discussing the limitations of
existing path tracking controllers in ROS2 and approaches for
introducing adaptiveness through RL (cf. Section II).
II. STATE OF THE ART ON PATH TRACKING
CONTROLLERS IN ROS2
ROS2 path tracking controllers can be classified as geometric, reactive, or model-predictive [12]. This section reviews
RPP, DWB, and MPPI as commonly-used examples of these
categories. We focus on their applicability to open, dynamic
environments, and discuss their limitations in adaptability,
performance, and applicability. As RL addresses these properties, we also discuss its potential in path tracking (cf. Section II-D) before concluding the section with a discussion

(cf. Section II-E).
A. Regulated Pure Pursuit (RPP)
RPP [4] is a geometric controller based on the pure pursuit
algorithm. It determines a so-called lookahead point on the
planned path at a specified lookahead distance (L) in front of
the robot. Then, it calculates the curvature and derives the
angular velocity from it. While the pure pursuit algorithm
fixes the linear velocity for that (the robot is always driving
at a constant speed [5]), the RPP incorporates a mechanism
that adjusts the linear and angular velocities as well as the
lookahead distance based on the robot’s distance to obstacles
and the path’s curvature. With that, the RPP is efficient
but lacks collision avoidance, hindering its adaptability in
dynamic environments. Furthermore, only the pure pursuit
algorithm (without its extensions) was analyzed regarding
its stability guarantees [13].
B. Dynamic Window Approach Version B (DWB)
DWB [2] is a reactive controller operating in two distinct
phases. First, it generates a set of candidate control actions by
sampling linear and angular velocities within a dynamic window of physically achievable velocities describing circular
trajectories. Only collision-free trajectories are considered.
Second, each candidate trajectory is evaluated using a cost
function that considers proximity to the goal, distance to obstacles, and current velocity. The control input corresponding
to the lowest-cost trajectory is then selected and applied to
the robot. While this approach integrates feasibility and basic
safety considerations, its reliance on a fixed cost function
necessitates careful tuning, which may be insufficient for
dynamically changing scenarios [12].
C. Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI)
MPPI [3], a model-predictive controller and a specialization
of reactive controllers, optimizes a cost function online by
sampling a search space. This allows it to not only consider
circular trajectories (as done by DWB) but also enables timely
reactions to changing environments. While MPPI does penalize unsafe behavior during optimization, it does not explicitly
encode safety constraints – they can still be violated. This can
potentially lead to suboptimal or unsafe solutions in complex
environments if misconfigured. Like DWB, MPPI’s parameters
are not adaptive, limiting its performance in dynamically
changing situations.
D. RL in Path Tracking
RL enables agents, that is, training-based controllers to
learn from interactions with their environment, adjusting
their actions based on rewards and penalties they receive.
By maximizing cumulative rewards over time, RL agents
can learn optimal control policies without requiring explicit
programming or supervision. Learning can be done online,
where the agent learns while interacting with the environment, or offline, where the agent learns from a dataset
of past interactions. Thus, even in complex and dynamic
environments, RL-based controllers can learn optimal control
policies that adapt to changing conditions [10].
Recent studies have explored various ways to apply RL
to path tracking. These include using a path-integral based
RL approach to learn optimal parameters for a path following controller offline and tune them online with realtime system states, leading to improved performance and
adaptability [14]. A hierarchical approach has also been
proposed by [8], where a high-level controller plans a path
based on a global map and a low-level controller uses RL to
track the path while avoiding obstacles in local, unknown environments. Q-learning has been combined with PID control
to improve tracking accuracy and reduce computational complexity in [9]. Another approach is proposed by [15]. They
developed an integrated kinematic and dynamic tracking control algorithm based on RL that does not require knowledge of
the robot’s dynamic model, leading to improved robustness
and adaptability [15]. Furthermore, their approach is the only
one of the listed that provides guarantees on the stability

potential in handling complex path tracking situations and
despite emerging approaches in safe RL [16], RL in general
still falls short in providing guarantees on safety or stability.
E. Discussion
Comparing traditional controllers readily implemented,
e.g., in ROS2, with recent RL approaches, highlights the
divergence between adaptability and safety. While RPP, DWB,
and MPPI provide reliable performance, they struggle to adapt
to dynamic conditions – even with complex, optimizationbased controllers such as MPPI. The challenge lies in the
precise configuration required to avoid unsafe behavior while
being able to handle complex environments. RL approaches,
on the other hand, offer adaptability and performance but
lack guarantees on stability or safety due to their black-box
nature and learning-based design. This seemingly contradictory nature raises the question: how can we combine the
adaptability of RL with the safety and stability of traditional
controllers?
III. THE SIMPLEX ARCHITECTURE
Hybrid architectures aim to combine different controllers
to exploit their individual characteristics. To address the
question of how to combine adaptability of, for instance, RLbased controllers, with the safety guarantees of traditional
controllers, we discuss the Simplex architecture [11] in
this section. After introducing its structure and components
(cf. Section III-A), we formulate our first contribution; design
considerations for providing stability and safety guarantees
in the context of the Simplex architecture (cf. Section III-B).
A. Components of the Simplex Architecture
The Simplex Architecture proposed by [11] combines
controllers to achieve safety while leveraging the performance advantages of less verifiable controllers. For that,
the architecture consists of three main components: a highperformance controller Cp(x), a high-assurance controller
Ca(x), and a decision module D (with x ∈X ⊆Rn being
the state of the system) as illustrated in Fig. 2. Together, they

realize a separation of concerns. The high-performance controller is designed for optimal performance, may be complex
and adaptive, and is not required to provide guarantees. The
high-assurance controller is designed to stabilize the system
and guarantee safety, potentially at the cost of performance.
The decision module acts as a switching mechanism between the two controllers, monitoring the system’s state and
the actions proposed by the high-performance controller. It
can perform two actions: (1) switch to the high-assurance
controller if the high-performance controller’s actions may
lead to unsafe behavior, and (2) switch back to the high-performance controller if the system is safe and stable. Thus,
while the high-assurance controller and decision module are
concerned with safety and stability, the high-performance
controller focuses on performance and adaptability.
B. Design Considerations for Stability and Safety
The separation of concerns in the Simplex architecture
provides a framework to achieve safety and stability but
requires careful design of the high-assurance controller and
the decision module. For that, the difference between safety
and stability needs to be clarified. Stability refers to the
system’s ability to return to a stable state after a disturbance,
while safety refers to the system’s ability to minimize the risk
of hazardous events by preventing entering associated states.
Thus, while stability is a necessary condition for safety, it is
not sufficient. For instance, a robot may stably follow a path
but still collide with an obstacle due to unsafe oscillations.
In this line, we discuss design considerations for the
high-assurance controller to provide stability guarantees and
the decision module to implement a strategy for switching
between the high-performance and high-assurance controller
to maintain system safety. We first discuss stability as a basis
of safety in Section III-B.1 to derive stability guarantees
for the high-assurance controller. Then, we integrate safety
constraints to derive a strategy for the decision module
to switch to the high-assurance controller when needed in
Section III-B.2. Finally, we discuss the concept of dwell
time [17], [18] in Section III-B.3 to derive a strategy for
safely switching back to the high-performance controller.
1) Stability Considerations: A necessary condition for
safety is stability. As the high-performance controller Cp(x)
does not provide stability guarantees and may even destabilize the system, the high-assurance controller Ca(x) needs to
ensure stability. Moreover, the assumptions and limitations
tied to these guarantees (e.g., as arising through linearization)
need to be explicitly known by the decision module since it
can only rely on the high-assurance controller to stabilize
the system when the assumptions hold. In other words,
the decision module needs to switch to the high-assurance
controller before control actions of the high-performance
controller Cp(x) drive the system to states where the stability
guarantees of Ca(x) are no longer valid. Thus, stability
for the Simplex architecture serves two purposes: ensuring
the high-assurance controller can stabilize the system and
providing a criterion for the decision module to switch to
the high-assurance controller.
A concept that can be applied here is the Region of Attraction (RoA), which defines the region XA|C ⊆X within the
state space where a controller C(x) is guaranteed to stabilize
the system. Determining the RoA can be achieved through
stability analysis methods, such as Lyapunov functions [19],
incremental stability [20], or reachability analysis [21]. These
approaches are suitable for non-linear systems as is the case
for path tracking.
Lyapunov functions are scalar functions that decrease
along system trajectories that converge towards an equilibrium point, providing a measure of the system’s energy [19].
Thus, a system is stable if it minimizes the Lyapunov
function. Its region of attraction is then defined as the level
set of the Lyapunov function. However, finding a Lyapunov
function for an arbitrary system can be challenging and leads
to conservative approximations of the actual RoA [19].
Incremental stability focuses on the convergence of any
two system trajectories, providing a measure of stability even
without a specific equilibrium point [20]. Assuming that a set
of states XI can be found for which the system’s trajectories
start and end in XI while converging over time, the set is
said to be forward invariant and can be interpreted as a RoA
(XI = XA|C). However, defining this forward invariant set
can be difficult, especially for non-linear systems. Reachability
analysis [21] approaches the problem by computing the
set of all possible states that can be reached within a finite
time, starting from an initial set. This is done by leveraging
the system’s dynamics and can provide a precise estimate of
the RoA. However, it is computationally expensive and requires
model knowledge, which may limit its applicability in complex,
real-world environments.

2) Safety Constraints: Safety in the context of the Simplex
architecture refers to the ability to prevent the system from
entering dangerous states. This can be achieved by enforcing
safety constraints on the high-performance controller or by
the decision module. The decision module can switch to the
high-assurance controller if the high-performance controller’s
actions may lead to unsafe states, ensuring that the system
remains within a safe operating space. For this, the decision
module needs to have access to a formal notion of safety, such
as a safe region in the state space where the system should
not enter.

3) Dwell Time: Dwell time refers to the minimum amount of
time that the decision module needs to stay in the high-performance
controller before switching back to the high-assurance
controller. It ensures that the high-performance controller does
not destabilize the system for too long, allowing the high-assurance
controller to re-establish stability. The dwell time can
be derived based on the system’s dynamics, the performance
of the high-performance controller, and the safety constraints
of the high-assurance controller. For instance, dwell time can
be determined by ensuring that the high-performance controller
does not deviate too far from the high-assurance controller’s
trajectory for too long, which would risk the system leaving
the region of attraction. Thus, dwell time provides a mechanism
for balancing performance and safety by capping the time
the high-performance controller can operate without the high-
assurance controller taking over.

IV. A SIMPLEX-BASED PATH TRACKING
CONTROLLER
In this section, we present a Simplex-based path tracking
controller that employs an RL-based high-performance controller
and a pure pursuit (PP)-based high-assurance controller. The
controller is evaluated in simulations (Section V), demonstrating
its effectiveness in maintaining safety while achieving comparable
performance to state-of-the-art methods, as well as in a
real-world deployment (Section VI).

A. High-Performance Controller (RL-based)
The RL-based controller operates under the assumption that
it can learn an optimal feedback policy for path tracking. We
utilize a path-integral reinforcement learning (PILRL) approach
[14] that allows the agent to learn from interaction with
the environment, optimizing a path integral reward function
that considers the distance to the goal, obstacle avoidance,
and smooth control inputs. The PILRL approach is chosen
because it enables the controller to learn in real-time without
prior knowledge of the robot’s dynamics, making it suitable
for complex and dynamic environments. The high-performance
controller Cp(x) is designed to maximize tracking performance,
while the high-assurance controller Ca(x) is responsible for
stabilizing the system and ensuring safety.

B. High-Assurance Controller (PP-based)
The pure pursuit controller is a classical approach for path
tracking that calculates a lookahead point on the planned
path based on a specified lookahead distance (L). The controller
then calculates the curvature and derives the angular
velocity from it. While the pure pursuit controller fixes the
linear velocity for the robot, the RPP incorporates a mechanism
that adjusts the linear and angular velocities as well as the
lookahead distance based on the robot’s distance to obstacles
and the path’s curvature. However, the pure pursuit controller
does not provide collision avoidance, hindering its adaptability
in dynamic environments. Moreover, only the pure pursuit
algorithm (without its extensions) was analyzed regarding
its stability guarantees [13].

C. Decision Module D
The decision module D is responsible for monitoring the
system’s state and the actions proposed by the high-performance
controller Cp(x). It can perform two actions: (1) switch to the
high-assurance controller Ca(x) if the high-performance controller’s
actions may lead to unsafe states, and (2) switch back to the
high-performance controller Cp(x) if the system is safe and stable.
Thus, while the high-performance controller is focused on
performance and adaptability, the high-assurance controller
and decision module are concerned with safety and stability.
The decision module can implement several strategies for
switching between the two controllers, such as based on the
system’s state, the performance of the high-performance controller,
or the safety constraints of the high-assurance controller.
